New investigation reveals 15,000 pigs suffering from extreme heat
This summer, Essere Animali monitored the transport of pigs to major slaughterhouses in Lombardy and Emilia-Romagna during extreme temperatures.
For the first time in Italy, the NGO used a thermal camera to clearly show the heat stress these animals are subjected to during heat-alert days, while waiting to enter slaughterhouses. Around 15,000 pigs were monitored and found to be suffering in dire conditions.
Internal truck temperatures recorded up to 45°C
Using a heat gun and a thermal imaging camera, Essere Animali recorded internal truck temperatures of up to 45°C.
All the animals observed showed problems consistent with heat stress, including breathing rapidly and salivating excessively, as well as having reddened skin.
The conditions on the trucks were also very concerning, and did little to alleviate the animals’ suffering. The following problems were documented:
- Insufficient bedding, with animals coming into direct contact with the metal floor of the trucks;
- No access to water in any of the trucks monitored,
- Being transported in dense groups, making transport during high temperatures even more uncomfortable;
- Fans being switched off during stops.
In addition, the NGO documented around ten dead pigs inside one slaughterhouse. Drone footage showed that at least one of them died during transport: capturing it being unloaded from the truck with a forklift, and placed in a container for slaughterhouse waste.
The climate crisis demands urgent regulatory action that can no longer be postponed
For national journeys of under eight hours, current legislation on live animal transport does not require compliance with maximum temperatures, nor does it require that animals have access to water – a very serious gap in the rules, which can cause tens of thousands of animals to suffer each year, especially in summer. Following its investigation, Essere Animali will be filing formal reports with the authorities against all parties involved.
It is unacceptable for animals to be transported during extreme temperatures without robust protections in place. The latest science, including an opinion by the European Food Safety Authority, supports this view.
As part of the EU’s update to its live transport laws, decision-makers should set strict limits on transporting animals during extreme temperatures, along with other measures to address long journeys, live exports to third countries, and more. Written over 20 years ago, the current rules are nowhere near strong enough to protect transported animals, including from the worsening climate conditions we all face today.

Penn State measured a green roof during a June 2002 heat spell; its membrane peaked near 30°C, while the uncovered roof surface climbed to nearly 70°C
Synopsis
Green roofs present a remarkable solution for enhancing temperature control in urban environments, effectively lowering surface temperatures. The vegetation on rooftops generates shade while aiding in air cooling through the process of evapotranspiration. This natural cooling not only alleviates indoor temperatures but also minimizes energy consumption. Across the country, federal agencies are increasingly adopting green roof systems, marking a strategic approach to mitigate summer cooling demands.
A typical roof absorbs a lot of heat when the sun comes out. Dark membranes and shingles absorb solar radiation, and the only way to escape the heat is to warm the building below and the air above. The Penn State team found the same pattern in another test on a hot day. With the air at about 32 degrees Celsius, an exposed black plastic surface reached about 63 degrees Celsius, while sedum plants on a green roof stayed near 28 degrees Celsius.
A green roof breaks that pattern through evapotranspiration. The US Environmental Protection Agency has observed the same effect nationwide. Their findings suggest that green roofs provide shade, cool the air, and lower temperatures in both the roof surface and the surrounding air. In contrast, conventional rooftop surfaces may exceed the air temperature.
The heat gap reaches the room below, not just the roof
Roof temperature does not stay on the roof. It moves into the ceiling and the rooms below. In the same June 2002 test, the average interior temperatures of buildings with bare roofs soared past 40 degrees Celsius, while the green-roofed buildings kept interior temperatures close to the outside air for most of the period.
A building topped with a lush green roof. Image Credit: Wikimedia Commons
The federal government is testing the same idea at scale
The U.S. General Services Administration now has more than 80 buildings with green roofs, covering 2.2 million square feet of roof space from coast to coast. One federal roof, after factoring in the costs of stormwater management, horticultural maintenance, and energy savings, had a payback period of six years on its initial investment. Over the roof's expected lifespan, GSA calculated a total return on investment of 224 percent. A government agency has reached the same conclusion as academic researchers about the energy-saving potential of planted roofs. The key point is not how much power a building with a green roof puts back into the grid, but how much energy it saves the owner.
What renters and homeowners can take from this
Most people will not install a rooftop garden, and a full roof retrofit is a major construction project. But the principles behind a green roof still apply on a smaller scale. Anything that shades a rooftop surface and keeps it from directly absorbing sunlight, from reflective coatings to potted plants on a level rooftop deck, can have similar physical effects to those documented by Penn State and the EPA. The EPA highlights cool roofs as a similar option, using reflective material rather than vegetation to provide some of the same benefits to surface temperatures while being cheaper to install and a viable choice for those who cannot afford a green roof. The research offers a practical lesson for anyone in an urban area facing rising summer electricity bills: a roof's color and covering directly affect how much heat enters the building below.
Green roofs are becoming a real cooling strategy for US buildings

Plants have a built-in cooling system for extreme heat
Researchers found the molecular pathway that helps plants open leaf pores in extreme heat, allowing water to evaporate and cool their leaves.
A plant in a drought seals the pores on its leaves and stops losing water. In a heat wave it has to do the opposite, opening those pores so water evaporates and the leaf cools. Researchers in Belgium have now traced what keeps them open in the heat, and it runs on the same signal that closes them in a drought.
The work ran in thale cress, a small weed plant labs use as a stand-in for bigger plants, and in baker’s yeast. A group at VIB in Ghent traced the heat response to a protein called UBP24 and to a single chemical tag stuck onto it. The tag is a phosphate group, and adding one makes a protein slightly more negative.
Leaf pores are a plant’s cooling system
An animal that gets too hot walks into the shade. A plant can’t, so it cools the way a sweating body does, by letting water evaporate off its surface.
That water leaves through microscopic pores on the underside of the leaf. Each has two curved cells beside it, and when those cells swell with water they bow apart and the pore widens.
Plants use the same pores to take in carbon dioxide, so how plants breathe and how they stay cool are one question.
To watch the pores react, the team peeled the skin off thale cress leaves and warmed the strips for two hours in the dark. The pores barely moved at 82°F (28°C). They opened at 95°F (35°C) and wider still at 108°F (42°C).
Heat alone was enough. No light, no wind, no soil.
One protein keeps the pores open
Cells mark worn-out proteins for destruction by clipping a small tag onto them. UBP24 is one of the proteins that takes those tags off.
Plants missing a working copy of UBP24 barely opened their pores at 108°F, and putting an intact copy of the gene back restored normal opening.
UBP24 protects a pump called AHA1, which sits in the outer membrane of those curved cells and pushes charged particles out, the first step in drawing water in. Switch UBP24 off and AHA1 collected more destruction tags, and less of it survived.
The team rebuilt AHA1 so cells could no longer tag it at the five key spots. That version rescued the pores in plants lacking UBP24. The ordinary version did not.
A drought signal switches roles
A protein called OPEN STOMATA 1 – or OST1 – tags UBP24. Plant biologists know OST1 for using a plant hormone called ABA to shut pores during drought.
Here it was doing the reverse, which the authors call a conflict with the accepted role of OST1.
Under heat, ABA levels in the pore cells didn’t rise. Plants treated with a chemical that blocks ABA production still opened their pores, as did a mutant that can barely make the hormone.
Instead, a family of seven other proteins turned OST1 on. Knock out all seven and the pores barely opened in the heat.
The switch appeared in vascular plants
Researchers then lined up the UBP24 gene from 55 species, from algae to flowering plants, and looked at the one spot where the tag goes.
Liverworts and some mosses have pores fixed in place. Vascular plants, the ones with internal plumbing, can work theirs.
Nearly all of them carry a taggable amino acid at that position, at about the same point in the tree as pores that open and close on demand.
Ive De Smet, who runs the group at the VIB-UGent center where the team did the work, told Earth.com that the timing caught them off guard. What surprised them was “the tight correlation with the appearance of stomatal dynamics in land plants,” he said.
Yeast uses a different heat switch
Baker’s yeast has no pores to open, but it has a close relative of UBP24 called Ubp3. At the equivalent position, Ubp3 has a permanently negative amino acid. It always carries the charge, so no tag is needed.
That amino acid rarely changes. Eight Saccharomyces species with different temperature preferences all share it, and in an earlier experiment yeast pushed from 77°F (25°C) to 104°F (40°C) over 600 generations never shifted it.
Swapping it for a neutral amino acid slowed the yeast down at every temperature tested, most of all at 68°F (20°C). The yeast side of the work was run with Kevin Verstrepen’s group at KU Leuven.
That was the result De Smet said he did not see coming, because “a single amino acid exchange was sufficient to alter yeast responsiveness to heat.”
Crop uses remain untested
The search that started all this compared thale cress seedlings with wheat, both warmed to about 95°F (35°C). Eight proteins picked up the same tag in both, UBP24 among them.
That is as close to a food crop as this work gets. Nothing was tested in a field, and the genetic fixes being tried in crops start from several different places.
De Smet said the finding “can now be used, for instance, in breeding programs or to introduce a mutation into crops through targeted genome editing.” His lab has also started a project with UHasselt’s Ecotron facility to test plants under a future climate scenario.
That is not a near-term prospect. “It will still require some time before this knowledge is incorporated in a crop to make it more heat resilient,” he said.
A bigger question is the one the authors raise themselves. They still can’t say how OST1 chooses between closing pores in drought and opening them in heat when a plant meets both at once.
De Smet’s own next step is to map the wider signaling network around UBP24, down to “the single cell level, namely in individual guard cells.”
The full study was published in the journal Nature Plants.

full_text:
Parents and teachers at schools across San Diego County are raising concerns about students learning in extremely hot classrooms as a heat wave pushes temperatures into the triple digits in some areas.
Thermometers have recorded classroom temperatures into the 90s, while parents and teachers at Gage Elementary School in San Carlos say broken air conditioning has left students sitting in the heat for hours without a cooler alternative.
Taylor Hammond, whose 6-year-old son attends Gage Elementary, said the heat is affecting his child.
“He comes home with heat rashes. He comes home complaining that his classroom is hot," Hammond said.
Hammond said his son's teacher has been struggling with the classroom conditions since the beginning of the school year and has sought help from families.
“His teacher basically was like, 'hey, can you guys help me? Like, I'm struggling. I'm bringing spray bottles from home to spray the kids down in the classroom.'"
Hammond said the teacher also asked parents to put pressure on administrators and bring fans into the classroom.
Local
“I just thought that was kind of bizarre," Hammond said.
According to Hammond, the classroom reached 89 degrees over the past two days, with even hotter conditions outside and very little breeze.
“Yesterday in this area, it was 106 degrees... I don't even leave my dog at home in that kind of temperature,” Hammond said.
Hammond said he contacted the school principal, the County Board of Education and the school district about his concerns. He said the district told him it would look into the situation.
San Diego Unified School District said its classrooms have air conditioning but acknowledged that malfunctions can occur when units work overtime during extreme heat.
The District released the following statement:
“San Diego Unified school classrooms have air conditioning, and during extreme heat when the units are working overtime malfunctions can happen. Our HVAC team has been working with the school directly to address the malfunction. Currently the classroom has working air conditioning, and the technician will be doing a status check on Friday."
"It’s important for families to understand alternative spaces with working air conditioners, including other classrooms and the library, have been made available to ensure the safety of our students and educators during this heat wave.”
Hammond said his son has not been moved to one of those alternative spaces.
“I thought maybe they would move him to another classroom, or they would kind of make sure that something was accommodated ... I understand that air conditioning breaks, you know, maintenance happens. There's backlog issues and I understand that. But I think it's been an unacceptable for the duration that it’s been going on," Hammond said.
Similar concerns have surfaced elsewhere in San Diego County. NBC San Diego has received reports of classrooms reaching 90 degrees in the Oceanside Unified School District. The district said it has multiple measures available, including portable air conditioners and fans to help keep classrooms cool.
This story was originally reported for broadcast by NBC San Diego. AI tools helped convert the story to a digital article, and an NBC San Diego journalist edited the article for publication.

title: Dehydration can sneak up faster than you think—and the warning signs are easy to dismiss - Yahoo Health
search_term: (heatstroke OR "heat stroke" OR sunstroke OR "heat exhaustion" OR "heat-related death" OR "heat casualty" OR "heat fatality" OR "suspected heat death" OR dehydration OR "heat cramps" OR "heat illness") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
Feeling a little dizzy or unusually tired on a hot day can seem harmless right up until your body can no longer compensate.
Singer Ray LaMontagne recently collapsed during a performance in Nashville, where temperatures outside had reached triple digits. His management later said he was being treated for heat-related dehydration.
It's an extreme example of something that can happen far more quietly to people gardening, exercising, traveling, attending outdoor events or simply spending too much time in the heat. Thirst isn't always the first—or best—warning that you're getting into trouble.
Heat makes your body work harder
Your body needs to maintain a relatively narrow internal temperature range. When you're hot, blood flow to the skin increases and sweating helps release heat through evaporation. But sweating also removes fluid. If you don't replace enough of it, blood volume can decrease and your cardiovascular system has to work harder.
High humidity complicates matters because sweat doesn't evaporate as efficiently, reducing one of the body's most important cooling mechanisms.
The early symptoms can seem ordinary
According to the CDC, signs that your body is overheating can include heavy sweating, dizziness, headache, weakness, nausea, shortness of breath and muscle cramps. Those symptoms are easy to rationalize. Maybe you didn't sleep well. Maybe you're hungry. Maybe you're just tired.
That's precisely why paying attention to the circumstances matters. If you're in significant heat and suddenly feel weak, dizzy or nauseated, don't assume you can simply push through it.
Heat exhaustion and heat stroke aren't the same
Heat-related illness exists on a spectrum. Heat exhaustion can involve heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea and headache. Heat stroke is much more dangerous. It occurs when the body loses its ability to control its temperature.
The CDC's occupational heat guidance warns that during heat stroke, body temperature can rise rapidly and the condition can cause permanent disability or death without emergency treatment. Confusion, altered behavior, fainting or loss of consciousness in the heat should therefore never be dismissed as ordinary dehydration.
You don't have to be exercising outdoors
Heat illness isn't limited to marathon runners and construction workers. Older adults can be especially vulnerable because thirst perception and temperature regulation can change with age. Certain medications and chronic medical conditions can also affect the body's response to heat. Indoor environments can become dangerous, too.
An apartment, workplace, performance space or house without adequate cooling can expose someone to significant heat even without direct sun.
Drinking ahead of thirst can help
During hot weather, the CDC recommends drinking fluids regularly rather than waiting until you're desperately thirsty. Water is sufficient for many everyday situations. People sweating heavily for prolonged periods may also need to replace electrolytes, although most people don't need sports drinks simply because the temperature climbed. Alcohol can make hydration more difficult, and people should also be mindful of excessive caffeine during significant heat exposure.
Urine color can offer a rough clue: pale yellow generally suggests better hydration than dark yellow urine, although medications, supplements and medical conditions can affect color.
The biggest mistake may be trying to tough it out
Heat illness can progress while someone keeps working, walking or exercising because they don't want to stop. But once dizziness, weakness or nausea appears, continuing to generate body heat can make matters worse. Get somewhere cooler. Rest. Drink fluids if you're conscious and able to do so. And seek emergency help for confusion, collapse, seizures, loss of consciousness or suspected heat stroke.
Heat doesn't care how fit you are or how determined you are to finish what you're doing. Sometimes the smartest thing you can do is stop.
Have you ever realized only after the fact that you'd become significantly dehydrated?

Eight Colombian capital cities remain on red alert due to risks associated with the El Niño phenomenon, mainly because of possible water shortages and an increase in vegetation fires.
The warning was issued by the Colombian Association of Capital Cities (Asocapitales), which identified Santa Marta, San Andres, Riohacha, Quibdo, Cucuta, Ibague, Neiva, and Pasto as the territories with the highest level of vulnerability to the weather conditions expected in the coming months.
The situation could worsen toward the end of the year. The Institute of Hydrology, Meteorology and Environmental Studies (Ideam) estimates that conditions associated with El Niño are highly likely to continue into early 2027 and warns that the period of greatest intensity will occur during the final months of 2026.
Between October and December, the phenomenon could reach a “very strong” intensity, increasing pressure on water supply systems and raising the risk of fires.
Eight Colombian cities on red alert as El Niño triggers water shortages and fires
The Urban Vulnerability Index for El Niño developed by Asocapitales shows that water shortages are currently the risk causing the greatest concern among local administrations. The organization said this threat accounts for 77% of the risks identified by the cities, while vegetation fires account for 64%.
The concern is not limited to the eight capitals classified as being at red alert level. In total, 17 cities are at orange risk level and another seven at yellow, reflecting widespread pressure across the territories as a phenomenon that can affect each region differently takes hold.
The warning signs are already visible in some cities. Medellin has experienced scheduled disruptions to water service in six districts due to difficulties related to water availability, while Cali is facing prolonged periods of drought and growing concern over wildfires.
In Leticia, although it is not among the eight capitals on red alert, the decline in the level of the Amazon River is raising concerns about its potential effects on water supplies and agricultural production.

Fires are already causing damage in different regions
The risk of fires is also beginning to translate into concrete impacts. According to the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management (UNGRD), wildfires recorded through August 26 had affected 78 people, damaged 14 homes, destroyed 10, and damaged one water supply system.
The impact on productive activities is also significant. Figures presented by the UNGRD indicate that 119,569 hectares of crops and productive systems have been affected by the conditions recorded.
For authorities, the problem could take on greater dimensions during the months when El Niño is expected to reach its peak intensity. Rising temperatures, declining rainfall, and deteriorating humidity conditions create a favorable environment for fires to spread and increase pressure on water sources.
Maximum concern for the end of 2026
Ideam maintains an especially concerning outlook for the final quarter of the year. According to the update presented to local authorities, there is a 90% probability that El Niño conditions will continue into early 2027, while the possibility that the event will reach exceptional intensity is also high.
Projections indicate that between October and December, the surface temperature of the Pacific Ocean could register an anomaly of up to 3.5°C. This behavior is one of the factors supporting the forecast of a particularly intense phase of the phenomenon.
The World Meteorological Organization, for its part, estimates a probability close to 100% that conditions associated with El Niño will persist through February 2027. This means cities will have to prepare not only for the end of this year, but also for possible impacts during the first months of next year.
Against this backdrop, Asocapitales and the UNGRD agreed to strengthen coordination between local administrations and the national government. The goal is to anticipate the effects on water supplies, fires, energy, public health, and productive activities.
Authorities will have to maintain constant monitoring of water sources and emergency response capacity while promoting responsible water use and fire prevention.
The combination of territorial alerts, the impacts already recorded, and climate projections keeps Colombia’s capital cities under a high level of surveillance. The most critical period has yet to begin and, according to official forecasts, could continue for several more months.
